prompt: `Encoding.java` wrote `Sertão` as UTF-8. How many bytes did the file hold?
hint: One letter is not from the plain alphabet.

choices.text: Seven: one per letter, two for `ã`
choices.why: Right: `c3 a3`.

choices.text: Six, one per character
choices.why: `ã` takes two.

choices.text: Twelve, two for every character
choices.why: That is UTF-16, which the file did not use.

choices.text: Eight, with a marker at the end of the text
choices.why: The capture lists every byte, and there is no marker.

prompt: The UTF-8 file was read back as ISO-8859-1. What happened?

choices.text: A `MalformedInputException` stopped the read
choices.why: Nothing was thrown.

choices.text: `SertÃ£o`, printed without an error or a warning
choices.why: Right: each byte became a character.

choices.text: The word came back whole, since Java 18 fixed it

choices.text: The `ã` was dropped and `Serto` came back
choices.why: Both of its bytes came back, as characters.

prompt: Which class turns an `InputStream` into a `Reader`?

choices.text: `InputStreamReader`
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `FileReader`
choices.why: That opens a file by name; it does not wrap a stream you hand it.

choices.text: `BufferedInputStream`
choices.why: That adds a buffer and stays a byte stream.

choices.text: `OutputStreamWriter`
choices.why: That is the bridge in the other direction.

prompt: Since Java 18 the platform's default encoding is ___ on every system.
hint: The one the lesson tells you to name.

prompt: In the capture, how many milliseconds did the buffered read of the 5 MB file take?
Why was the unbuffered read so much slower, with the same loop?

choices.text: The sum overflowed and had to be recomputed
choices.why: Both sums are the same and fit in a `long`.

choices.text: Each `read()` was a separate trip into the kernel
choices.why: Right: over five million of them.

choices.text: `FileInputStream` decodes every byte as UTF-8
choices.why: It moves bytes and decodes nothing.

choices.text: The disk had to spin up for the first one
choices.why: The file was written a moment before, and the gap is per byte.

prompt: A program writes a report through a `BufferedWriter`, never closes it, and exits. What is in the file?
hint: Where the last characters still are.

choices.text: Only what had already been written out before the end
choices.why: Right: the rest was still in memory.

choices.text: The whole report, since exiting flushes every buffer
choices.why: Nothing flushes a Java buffer at exit.

choices.text: Nothing at all; the file is not even created
choices.why: Opening the stream creates the file.

choices.text: The report followed by the buffer's unused bytes
choices.why: Unused room is never written.

prompt: Put the layers of `Layers.java` in order, from the file outwards.
With `ulimit -n 64`, which `FileInputStream` did `Leak.java` fail to open?
hint: The JVM holds some descriptors itself.

choices.text: The 65th
choices.why: The JVM had already taken some.

choices.text: The 61st
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The 101st, after the loop
choices.why: The loop stops at 100.

choices.text: The first: the limit was too low
choices.why: Sixty of them opened.

prompt: A `BufferedReader` wraps an `InputStreamReader`, which wraps a `FileInputStream`. What should the code close?
hint: Each one closes what it wraps.

choices.text: Only the `FileInputStream`, which holds the file
choices.why: That skips what the outer layers hold.

choices.text: Nothing, as the garbage collector closes them
choices.why: Maybe, and maybe never.

choices.text: All three, from the inside out
choices.why: Closing the inner ones first leaves the outer buffer pointing at a closed stream.

choices.text: Only the outermost, the `BufferedReader`
choices.why: Right: its `close` reaches the other two.

prompt: A server leaks one descriptor per request. Where does `Too many open files` appear?
hint: Who asks for the next one?

choices.text: At the line that forgot to close
choices.why: That line succeeded every time.

choices.text: At start-up, before the first request
choices.why: The limit is reached after thousands.

choices.text: In the garbage collector's log
choices.why: It arrives as an `IOException` in the program.

choices.text: In whatever code opens the next file or socket
choices.why: Right: often far from the leak.

prompt: `java WordCount.java < /dev/null 2> errors.txt` printed one line. Where did the warning go?

choices.text: Into `errors.txt`, where `cat` found it
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Nowhere: `/dev/null` swallowed it
choices.why: `/dev/null` was the input.

choices.text: Into the count, on standard output
choices.why: The count line was printed alone.

choices.text: It belongs to the process, not to `main`
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Closing it throws an `IOException`
choices.why: It can be closed.

choices.text: The shell closes it before the program starts

choices.text: A `BufferedReader` around it closes it already

prompt: Match each job with the stream to use.
hint: Bytes or characters, and the bridge between them.

prompt: Which of these leak a file descriptor? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: `try (var in = new FileInputStream(f)) { in.read(); }`
choices.why: No: the `try` closes it.

choices.text: `new FileInputStream(f).read()` in a loop
choices.why: Yes: nothing closes it.

choices.text: A `BufferedReader` kept in a field and never closed
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: `Files.readString(path)`
choices.why: No: it opens and closes the file itself.
